## 解法
Using the linear-space approach.

Let \(V=\{f(x)\in \mathbb P_3[x]: f'(5)=f(1)\}\) and define \(L:\mathbb P_3[x]\to\mathbb R\) by \(L(f)=f'(5)-f(1)\). Evaluation at a point and differentiation are linear, hence \(L\) is linear. Clearly \(V=\ker L\).

The space \(\mathbb P_3[x]\) of polynomials of degree \(<3\) has standard basis \(\{1,x,x^2\}\), so \(\dim \mathbb P_3[x]=3\). Since \(L(1)=0-1=-1\ne0\), \(L\) is not the zero functional; thus its image is \(\mathbb R\) and \(\dim\operatorname{im}L=1\). By rank-nullity:
\[
\dim V=\dim\ker L=3-1=2.
\]
Thus a basis has two elements.

Now take an arbitrary \(f(x)=a x^2+b x+c\in \mathbb P_3[x]\). Then \(f'(x)=2a x+b\). The condition is
\[
f'(5)=f(1)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
10a+b=a+b+c
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
c=9a.
\]
So every \(f\in V\) has the form
\[
f(x)=a x^2+b x+9a=a(x^2+9)+b x.
\]
Hence \(V=\operatorname{span}\{x^2+9,x\}\). The two polynomials are linearly independent: if \(\alpha(x^2+9)+\beta x=0\), comparing the \(x^2\)-coefficient gives \(\alpha=0\), and then \(\beta=0\). Therefore \(\{x^2+9,x\}\) is a basis.

## 题目
Find a basis \(\{p(x), q(x)\}\) for the vector space \(\{f(x)\in \mathbb P_3[x] \mid f'(5)=f(1)\}\), where \(\mathbb P_3[x]\) is the vector space of polynomials in \(x\) with degree less than 3. \(p(x)=\) [ANS], \(q(x)=\) [ANS].

## 解法
Using the linear-space approach.

Define \(L:\mathbb P_3[x]\to \mathbb R\) by \(L(f)=f'(5)-f(1)\). Since differentiation and evaluation are linear, L is linear. Then V = ker L.

The space \(\mathbb P_3[x]\) has basis \(\{1,x,x^2\}\), so dim = 3. \(L(1)=0-1=-1\ne 0\), so L is not zero; hence \(\operatorname{im} L = \mathbb R\) and dim im L =1. Rank-nullity gives:
\[
\dim V = \dim \ker L = 3-1=2.
\]
Thus need two polynomials.

For \(f(x)=a x^2 + b x + c\), \(f'(x)=2a x+b\). Then condition:
\[
f'(5)=f(1) \iff 10a+b=a+b+c \iff c=9a.
\]
Thus every \(f\in V\) can be written as:
\[
f(x)=a x^2+b x+9a=b x+a(x^2+9).
\]
So \(V=\operatorname{span}\{x,x^2+9\}\). These polynomials are linearly independent because a nonzero linear combination \(\lambda x+\mu(x^2+9)=0\) would have \(\mu=0\) from the \(x^2\) coefficient, then \(\lambda=0\). Hence basis.

Find a basis \(\{p(x), q(x)\}\) for the vector space \(\{f(x)\in\mathbb P_3[x]\mid f'(5)=f(1)\}\), where \(\mathbb P_3[x]\) is the vector space of polynomials in \(x\) with degree less than 3. \(p(x)=\) [ANS], \(q(x)=\) [ANS].

## 解法
Using the linear-space approach.

Let \(V = \{f \in \mathbb P_3[x] : f'(5)=f(1)\}\). Define \(L:\mathbb P_3[x]\to \mathbb R\) by \(L(f)=f'(5)-f(1)\). Differentiation and evaluation are linear, so \(L\) is linear, and \(V=\ker L\).

The space \(\mathbb P_3[x]\) has basis \(\{1,x,x^2\}\), so \(\dim \mathbb P_3[x]=3\). Since \(L(1)=0-1=-1\ne0\), \(L\) is not zero, hence \(\operatorname{im}L=\mathbb R\). By rank-nullity,
\[
\dim V=\dim\ker L=3-1=2.
\]
Thus any basis of \(V\) consists of two polynomials.

For \(f(x)=a x^2+b x+c\),
\[
f'(x)=2a x+b,\quad f'(5)=10a+b,\quad f(1)=a+b+c.
\]
Thus
\[
f'(5)=f(1)\iff 10a+b=a+b+c\iff c=9a.
\]
Therefore every \(f\in V\) has the form
\[
f(x)=a x^2+b x+9a=b x+a(x^2+9),
\]
